q: Four alcohols are shaken separately with Lucas reagent at room temperature. Which one turns the mixture cloudy at once?
x: Tertiary alcohols form a stable carbocation and are converted to the insoluble chloride immediately. Secondary alcohols such as butan-2-ol take about five minutes, and primary alcohols do not react noticeably at room temperature.

q: Glucose is fermented by yeast: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. What mass of ethanol can be obtained from 90 g of glucose? (C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180, C₂H₅OH = 46 g mol⁻¹)
x: 90/180 = 0.5 mol glucose gives 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 mol ethanol = 46 g. Ignoring the 1:2 ratio gives 23 g; 44 g is the mass of CO₂ formed, not ethanol.

q: Ethanol is warmed with ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. The sweet-smelling product is:
x: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid give an ester and water (esterification): CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, with H₂SO₄ as catalyst. Ethoxyethane and ethene form from ethanol and H₂SO₄ alone, without the acid.

q: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI). The final organic product is:
x: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to the aldehyde; under reflux with excess oxidant the propanal cannot escape and is oxidised further to CH₃CH₂COOH. Propanal is obtained only if it is distilled off as it forms; propanone comes from propan-2-ol.

q: Sodium ethoxide, C₂H₅ONa, is added to water. It reacts to form ethanol and sodium hydroxide. This shows that:
o: Ethanol is a weaker acid than water
Ethanol is a stronger acid than water
The ethoxide ion is a weaker base than the hydroxide ion
Sodium ethoxide is an oxidising agent
x: C₂H₅O⁻ takes H⁺ from H₂O, so the reaction goes to the weaker acid (ethanol) and weaker base (OH⁻). Ethoxide is therefore the stronger base, and ethanol the weaker acid. Reading the equation backwards gives the tempting wrong choices.

q: An alcohol C₄H₁₀O gives no cloudiness with Lucas reagent at room temperature. Oxidation with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ gives a carboxylic acid with a branched carbon chain. The alcohol is:
x: No reaction with Lucas reagent and oxidation to an acid both point to a primary alcohol. The two primary C₄ alcohols are butan-1-ol (straight chain, giving butanoic acid) and (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH (giving branched (CH₃)₂CHCOOH). Butan-2-ol gives a ketone, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised and reacts with Lucas reagent at once.

q: Equal amounts of methanol, a primary, a secondary and a tertiary alcohol are added to sodium. The usual order of decreasing rate of hydrogen evolution is:
x: Alkyl groups push electron density towards oxygen and make the O–H less acidic, and they also hinder solvation of the alkoxide ion, so acidity and the rate with sodium fall from CH₃OH to tertiary alcohols. The reversed order is the Lucas test order, which depends on carbocation stability.

q: Phenol is treated with concentrated nitric acid (in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid). The main product is:
x: The –OH group strongly activates the ring, so with concentrated acid all three ortho and para positions are nitrated. Dilute nitric acid gives only the mononitrophenols; –OH is not a meta director.

q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through a clear aqueous solution of sodium phenoxide. The solution turns milky as phenol separates. This shows that:
o: Phenol is a stronger acid than carbonic acid
Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid
Sodium phenoxide is insoluble in water
x: CO₂ + H₂O gives H₂CO₃, which gives H⁺ to C₆H₅O⁻, freeing phenol; a stronger acid displaces a weaker one from its salt. This is also why phenol does not liberate CO₂ from NaHCO₃.

q: Phenol is treated with bromine dissolved in carbon disulphide (CS₂) at a low temperature. The main products are:
x: In a non-polar solvent at low temperature the ring is less activated (phenol is not ionised) and only one bromine substitutes, at the ortho or para position. Bromine water, a polar solvent, gives the white 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

q: Phenol reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl. The organic product is:
x: The O–H of phenol is acylated: C₆H₅OH + CH₃COCl → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl, an ester. Ethyl benzoate has the acid and alcohol parts the other way round; the C–O bond of phenol does not break, so chlorobenzene does not form.

q: The –OH group makes the benzene ring of phenol much more reactive towards electrophiles than benzene. The reason is that:
o: Oxygen withdraws electrons from the ring by its high electronegativity
The –OH group makes the ring lose its delocalised π system
The hydrogen of –OH is transferred to the electrophile
A lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising the electron density at the ortho and para positions
x: Resonance donation (+M) of an oxygen lone pair outweighs oxygen's inductive withdrawal, so the ring is activated, especially at ortho and para. Inductive withdrawal alone would deactivate the ring.

q: A compound C₇H₈O reacts with sodium to give hydrogen, does not dissolve in aqueous NaOH, and gives no colour with neutral FeCl₃ solution. The compound is:
x: Reaction with Na shows an O–H group, so it is not the ether methoxybenzene. The methylphenols are acidic enough to dissolve in NaOH and give a colour with FeCl₃. Phenylmethanol has its –OH on a CH₂ group, so it behaves as an alcohol.

q: A mixture of 4.7 g phenol and 4.6 g ethanol is shaken with 1.0 mol dm⁻³ aqueous NaOH. What volume of the NaOH solution reacts with the mixture? (C₆H₅OH = 94, C₂H₅OH = 46 g mol⁻¹)
x: Only phenol is acidic enough to react with aqueous NaOH: 4.7/94 = 0.050 mol, needing 0.050 mol NaOH = 50 cm³. Including the 0.10 mol ethanol gives 150 cm³; using only the ethanol gives 100 cm³.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
x: In IUPAC naming of ethers the larger alkyl group gives the parent alkane (propane) and the smaller one becomes the alkoxy substituent (ethoxy) on carbon 1. 1-Propoxyethane takes the smaller group as the parent; 2-ethoxypropane and 1-methoxybutane are isomers with different structures.

q: In methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, the C–O–C bond angle is about:
x: Oxygen is sp³ hybridised with two lone pairs, so the angle is near tetrahedral; the two bulky methyl groups push it slightly wider than in water, to about 110°. 104.5° is the H–O–H angle in water.

q: Methoxyethane, CH₃OC₂H₅, is treated with one mole of cold concentrated HI. The products are:
x: HI protonates the ether oxygen, and I⁻ then attacks the less hindered carbon (SN2), the methyl group, so CH₃I and C₂H₅OH form. Both iodides form only with excess hot HI; iodoethane and methanol would need attack at the more crowded ethyl carbon.

q: In the Williamson synthesis, C₂H₅O⁻Na⁺ + CH₃Br → C₂H₅OCH₃ + NaBr, the ethoxide ion acts as:
o: A nucleophile that replaces bromide by SN2 substitution
An electrophile that adds to the C–Br bond
A base that removes a hydrogen to form an alkene
A reducing agent that removes bromine
x: The negatively charged oxygen attacks the δ+ carbon of CH₃Br from the back and pushes out Br⁻ in one step. With bromomethane there is no β-hydrogen, so elimination cannot compete.

q: Ethanol reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen, but ethoxyethane does not. The reason is that ethoxyethane:
o: Has no lone pairs on its oxygen atom
Is a stronger acid than ethanol
Has no hydrogen atom bonded to oxygen
Has a higher boiling point than ethanol
x: Sodium releases H₂ only from O–H (acidic) hydrogens. In C₂H₅OC₂H₅ all hydrogens are on carbon. The ether oxygen still has two lone pairs, and ether boils lower than ethanol.

q: Excess ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. What is the greatest mass of ethoxyethane that 9.2 g of ethanol can give? (C₂H₅OH = 46, C₂H₅OC₂H₅ = 74 g mol⁻¹)
x: 9.2/46 = 0.20 mol ethanol; two molecules form one ether molecule, so 0.10 mol × 74 = 7.4 g. Ignoring the 2:1 ratio gives 14.8 g; 9.2 g assumes mass is unchanged and forgets the water lost.

q: A compound X, C₄H₁₀O, does not react with sodium. When heated with excess concentrated HI it gives only one organic product. X is:
x: No reaction with Na means no O–H, so X is an ether. Excess hot HI converts both alkyl groups into alkyl iodides; only a symmetrical ether, C₂H₅OC₂H₅, gives a single product (iodoethane). The methoxypropanes give iodomethane plus a propyl iodide.
